claim: Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome is caused by a thymidine substitution mutation at cytidine 608 (GGC >GGT), within exon 11 of the gene that encodes for Lamin A (LMNA).
source: HGPS is caused by a thymidine substitution mutation at cytidine 608 (GGC >GGT), within exon 11 of the gene that encodes for Lamin A (LMNA) (De Sandre-Giovannoli et al., 2003; Eriksson et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (De Sandre-Giovannoli et al., 2003; Eriksson et al., 2003).

claim: The LMNA mutation in HGPS induces the usage of a cryptic splice site and the subsequent deletion of 50 amino acids at the C terminus.
source: The mutation does not result in an amino acid substitution, frame shift or early termination. Rather, it induces the usage of a cryptic splice site and the subsequent deletion of 50 amino acids at the C terminus.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about the molecular mechanism of the LMNA mutation.

claim: The deletion of 50 amino acids impedes downstream processing of the protein and results in conservation of C terminus farnesylation.
source: In turn, this deletion impedes downstream processing of the protein and results in conservation of C terminus farnesylation (Davies et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Davies et al., 2009.

claim: The abnormal protein product resulting from the LMNA mutation is called Progerin.
source: This abnormal protein product is called Progerin.
evidence: The claim is stated as established nomenclature in the field.

claim: Aggregation of Progerin leads to a disruption of the normal nuclear envelope meshwork, leading to deformed nuclei, nuclear stiffening, and defective mechanotransduction.
source: Aggregation of Progerin leads to a disruption of the normal nuclear envelope meshwork, leading to deformed nuclei, nuclear stiffening, and defective mechanotransduction (Apte et al., 2017; Goldman et al., 2004; Lammerding et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Apte et al., 2017; Goldman et al., 2004; Lammerding et al., 2004).

claim: Average life expectancy for HGPS patients is 13.4 years.
source: Average life expectancy for HPGS patients is 13.4 years, with myocardial infarction and stroke being the predominant causes of death (Foundation, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Foundation, 2019.

claim: Myocardial infarction and stroke are the predominant causes of death in HGPS patients.
source: Average life expectancy for HPGS patients is 13.4 years, with myocardial infarction and stroke being the predominant causes of death (Foundation, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Foundation, 2019.

claim: HGPS patients appear normal at birth.
source: Patients appear normal at birth, with a disease onset around 2 years of age when they present with slow growth rate, short stature, and marked lipodystrophy with a characteristic loss of subcutaneous fat.
evidence: The claim is stated as established clinical knowledge about HGPS presentation.

claim: HGPS disease onset occurs around 2 years of age.
source: Patients appear normal at birth, with a disease onset around 2 years of age when they present with slow growth rate, short stature, and marked lipodystrophy with a characteristic loss of subcutaneous fat.
evidence: The claim is stated as established clinical knowledge about HGPS presentation.

claim: HGPS patients present with slow growth rate, short stature, and marked lipodystrophy with a characteristic loss of subcutaneous fat.
source: Patients appear normal at birth, with a disease onset around 2 years of age when they present with slow growth rate, short stature, and marked lipodystrophy with a characteristic loss of subcutaneous fat.
evidence: The claim is stated as established clinical knowledge about HGPS presentation.

claim: With progression, HGPS patients experience arthritis, joint contracture, osteoporosis and stiffening of blood vessels.
source: With progression, patients experience arthritis, joint contracture, osteoporosis and stiffening of blood vessels.
evidence: The claim is stated as established clinical knowledge about HGPS progression.

claim: Progeria patients present with various defects in all tissues of the mesenchymal lineage.
source: Of particular interest, progeria patients present with various defects in all tissues of the mesenchymal lineage.
evidence: The claim is stated as established clinical knowledge about HGPS.

claim: HGPS patients show reduced stature, generalized osteopenia, thin calvaria, and clavicle regression with absence of medial and lateral ends, as well as resorption of the distal bony phalanges and anterior ribs.
source: Specifically, regarding bone physiology, patients show reduced stature, generalized osteopenia, thin calvaria, and clavicle regression with absence of medial and lateral ends, as well as resorption of the distal bony phalanges and anterior ribs (Chawla et al., 2017; Cleveland et al., 2012; Gordon et al., 2011; Nazir et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Chawla et al., 2017; Cleveland et al., 2012; Gordon et al., 2011; Nazir et al., 2017).

claim: At birth, bone structure appears normal in HGPS patients.
source: These phenotypes are more striking when considering that at birth, bone structure appears normal.
evidence: The claim is stated as established clinical knowledge about HGPS.

claim: Fibroblasts from progeria patients showed abnormal levels of aggrecan, a marker of chondrogenic differentiation.
source: Previous observations, where fibroblasts from progeria patients showed abnormal levels of aggrecan (Lemire et al., 2006) a marker of chondrogenic differentiation, led us to hypothesize that fibroblasts derived from HGPS patients – themselves a cell of the mesenchymal lineage – could harbor vestigial transcriptional signatures to abnormal mesenchymal stem cell commitment, which would become apparent by comparing them with different normal age group controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lemire et al., 2006.

claim: This study analyzed 33 HGPS fibroblast datasets from 21 patients aged 1–20 years old.
source: By comparing the transcriptional profile of HPGS fibroblasts (33 datasets, 21 patients, 1–20 years old) with fibroblasts derived from age-matched controls (21 datasets, 16 donors, 1–19 years old), healthy adults, (16 donors, 26–43 years old) and healthy old adults (15 donors, 80–96 years old), we provide insight into important defects in repair biology, metabolism (calcium, lipid), and other areas important to the mesenchymal cell lineage.
evidence: The claim describes the dataset composition used in the study.

claim: This study analyzed 21 age-matched control fibroblast datasets from 16 donors aged 1–19 years old.
source: By comparing the transcriptional profile of HPGS fibroblasts (33 datasets, 21 patients, 1–20 years old) with fibroblasts derived from age-matched controls (21 datasets, 16 donors, 1–19 years old), healthy adults, (16 donors, 26–43 years old) and healthy old adults (15 donors, 80–96 years old), we provide insight into important defects in repair biology, metabolism (calcium, lipid), and other areas important to the mesenchymal cell lineage.
evidence: The claim describes the dataset composition used in the study.

claim: This study analyzed healthy adult fibroblasts from 16 donors aged 26–43 years old.
source: By comparing the transcriptional profile of HPGS fibroblasts (33 datasets, 21 patients, 1–20 years old) with fibroblasts derived from age-matched controls (21 datasets, 16 donors, 1–19 years old), healthy adults, (16 donors, 26–43 years old) and healthy old adults (15 donors, 80–96 years old), we provide insight into important defects in repair biology, metabolism (calcium, lipid), and other areas important to the mesenchymal cell lineage.
evidence: The claim describes the dataset composition used in the study.

claim: This study analyzed healthy old adult fibroblasts from 15 donors aged 80–96 years old.
source: By comparing the transcriptional profile of HPGS fibroblasts (33 datasets, 21 patients, 1–20 years old) with fibroblasts derived from age-matched controls (21 datasets, 16 donors, 1–19 years old), healthy adults, (16 donors, 26–43 years old) and healthy old adults (15 donors, 80–96 years old), we provide insight into important defects in repair biology, metabolism (calcium, lipid), and other areas important to the mesenchymal cell lineage.
evidence: The claim describes the dataset composition used in the study.

claim: Transcription of genes involved in negative regulation of chondrocyte commitment is compromised in fibroblasts from patients that are at the age of onset of postnatal endochondral ossification.
source: Our results show that transcription of genes involved in negative regulation of chondrocyte commitment is compromised in fibroblasts from patients that are at the age of onset of postnatal endochondral ossification.
evidence: The claim is a primary finding from the RNA-seq analysis presented in the study.

claim: PTHLH, BMP4, FZD4, and IGF1 show either abnormal genomic architecture or lamin associated domain alterations.
source: We report that some genes central to differentiation commitment into the chondrogenic-osteogenic lineage and identified as misregulated in this study (PTHLH, BMP4, FZD4, and IGF1) show either abnormal genomic architecture or lamin associated domain alterations.
evidence: The claim is a primary finding from the Hi-C and LAD analysis presented in the study.

claim: Before batch correction, RNA-seq datasets clustered according to laboratory of origin regardless of diagnosis.
source: When the resulting transcriptomics data were analyzed by principal component analysis (PCA), datasets clustered according to laboratory of origin regardless of diagnosis, making direct comparisons impossible (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), as has been previously observed in Progeria transcriptomics analysis (Ikegami et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and cited previous observation (Ikegami et al., 2020).

claim: After batch effect correction, the first principal component was able to segregate the samples depending on progeria/non progeria origin.
source: However, after batch effect correction (materials and methods Zhang et al., 2020a), the first principal component was able to segregate the samples depending on progeria/non progeria origin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) which enabled direct comparisons between patients and controls from different age groups which originated from different sources.
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and the batch correction method (Zhang et al., 2020a).

claim: Teenage HGPS patients showed the smallest number of genes changing expression levels when compared to age-matched controls.
source: Teenage HGPS patients showed the smallest number of genes changing expression levels when compared to age-matched controls, but the highest number of genes up/down regulated when compared to healthy middle-aged or old adults (Table 1 and Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: Teenage HGPS patients showed the highest number of genes up/down regulated when compared to healthy middle-aged or old adults.
source: Teenage HGPS patients showed the smallest number of genes changing expression levels when compared to age-matched controls, but the highest number of genes up/down regulated when compared to healthy middle-aged or old adults (Table 1 and Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: Comparisons between the normal children cohort and the adult normal controls yield few significant changes.
source: Importantly, comparisons between the normal children cohort and the adult normal controls yield few significant changes, suggesting that HGPS is the driver of the differences observed among cohorts.
evidence: The claim is supported by the differential expression analysis results.

claim: HGPS is the driver of the differences observed among cohorts.
source: Importantly, comparisons between the normal children cohort and the adult normal controls yield few significant changes, suggesting that HGPS is the driver of the differences observed among cohorts.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that normal age groups show few differences while HGPS samples show many differences.

source: Table 1. Number of up/down-regulated genes per age comparisons.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in Table 1.

claim: Gene ontology terms identified in the study pertain to eight functional clusters: DNA maintenance and Epigenetics, Repair and Extracellular matrix, Bone, Adipose Tissue, Blood Vessels, and Muscle.
source: Overall, relevant gene ontology terms identified in the study pertain to eight functional clusters: DNA maintenance and Epigenetics (Figure 1), Repair and Extracellular matrix (Figure 2), Bone (Figure 3), Adipose Tissue (Figure 4), Blood Vessels (Figure 5), and Muscle (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim summarizes the gene ontology analysis results shown in Figures 1-6.

claim: Nine hundred and seventy genes were related to the biological processes of epigenetic programming and DNA maintenance.
source: The largest number of differentially expressed genes (Nine hundred and seventy) were related to the biological processes of epigenetic programming and DNA maintenance (Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Gene ontology pathways in the DNA maintenance cluster include epigenetic regulation of gene silencing, senescence-associated heterochromatin, DNA repair, DNA recombination, and histone methylation/modifications.
source: Gene ontology pathways included in this cohort include epigenetic regulation of gene silencing, senescence-associated heterochromatin, DNA repair, DNA recombination, and histone methylation/modifications.
evidence: The claim describes the gene ontology categories identified in the analysis.

claim: DNA maintenance and epigenetics genes were predominantly over-expressed in young progeria patients when compared to all controls.
source: These genes were predominantly over-expressed in young progeria patients when compared to all controls (Figure 1B,C) and between teenaged patients compared to their age matched control and adults (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the heatmap and gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: DNA maintenance and epigenetics genes were over-expressed between teenaged patients compared to their age matched control and adults.
source: These genes were predominantly over-expressed in young progeria patients when compared to all controls (Figure 1B,C) and between teenaged patients compared to their age matched control and adults (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the heatmap and gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 1B,D.

claim: Epigenetic and DNA repair misregulation in Progeria has been extensively documented in previous evidence.
source: This is in line with extensive previous evidence of epigenetic and DNA repair misregulation in Progeria (Aguado et al., 2019; Gonzalo and Coll-Bonfill, 2019; Misteli and Scaffidi, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Aguado et al., 2019; Gonzalo and Coll-Bonfill, 2019; Misteli and Scaffidi, 2005).

claim: 585 genes related to tissue repair are differentially expressed between cohorts.
source: The next biological process with the most misregulated transcription among age groups was tissue repair. It bears mentioning that most of the nucleosome-associated proteins and histones identified in the DNA maintenance cluster, as previously described, overlap with the repair GO terms. In all, 585 genes are differentially expressed between cohorts (Figure 2A), with HGPS patients predominantly overexpressing targets pertaining to the organization of the extracellular matrix (145 genes, Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: HGPS patients predominantly overexpress 145 genes pertaining to the organization of the extracellular matrix.
source: In all, 585 genes are differentially expressed between cohorts (Figure 2A), with HGPS patients predominantly overexpressing targets pertaining to the organization of the extracellular matrix (145 genes, Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Signatures related to coagulation, Bone Morphogenic Protein signaling, and response to wound healing are all downregulated in young HGPS patients when compared to adults.
source: Interestingly, signatures related to coagulation, Bone Morphogenic Protein signaling, and response to wound healing are all downregulated in young HGPS patients when compared to adults (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 165 genes involved in bone biology are misregulated in HGPS fibroblasts.
source: Specifically, we see misregulation of transcription of genes involved in bone (165 genes. Figure 3), fat (261 genes. Figure 4), blood vessel homeostasis (131 genes. Figure 5), and muscle (261 genes. Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: 261 genes involved in fat biology are misregulated in HGPS fibroblasts.
source: Specifically, we see misregulation of transcription of genes involved in bone (165 genes. Figure 3), fat (261 genes. Figure 4), blood vessel homeostasis (131 genes. Figure 5), and muscle (261 genes. Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: 131 genes involved in blood vessel homeostasis are misregulated in HGPS fibroblasts.
source: Specifically, we see misregulation of transcription of genes involved in bone (165 genes. Figure 3), fat (261 genes. Figure 4), blood vessel homeostasis (131 genes. Figure 5), and muscle (261 genes. Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: 261 genes involved in muscle biology are misregulated in HGPS fibroblasts.
source: Specifically, we see misregulation of transcription of genes involved in bone (165 genes. Figure 3), fat (261 genes. Figure 4), blood vessel homeostasis (131 genes. Figure 5), and muscle (261 genes. Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: HGPS patients show phenotypes like osteopenia, early atherosclerosis, and lack of subcutaneous fat deposition.
source: All these lineages have been observed as compromised in HGPS patients, showing phenotypes like osteopenia, early atherosclerosis, and lack of subcutaneous fat deposition. (Gordon et al., 2011; Hamczyk et al., 2018; Xiong et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Gordon et al., 2011; Hamczyk et al., 2018; Xiong et al., 2013).

claim: Bone biology mis-regulation in HGPS appears to be stratified into two distinct hubs: downregulation of pathways related to calcium homeostasis and transport and upregulation of pathways involved in cell differentiation of chondrocytes and osteoblasts.
source: Bone biology mis-regulation appears to be stratified into two distinct hubs: downregulation of pathways related to calcium homeostasis and transport and upregulation of pathways involved in cell differentiation of chondrocytes and osteoblasts (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Comparing young patients' transcriptional profile to that of old adult normal controls shows upregulation of genes involved in late osteogenic commitment.
source: Comparing young patients' transcriptional profile to that of old adult normal controls shows upregulation of genes involved in late osteogenic commitment. Such is the case of ontology terms that include osteoblast differentiation, ossification, and chondrocyte differentiation (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Genes included in pathways related to cation homeostasis, particularly calcium, are downregulated in young HGPS patients compared to old adult controls.
source: In parallel, genes included in pathways related to cation homeostasis, particularly calcium, are downregulated (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Young HGPS samples show downregulation in pathways involving fat cell differentiation when compared to age-matched controls.
source: Young HGPS samples show downregulation in pathways involving fat cell differentiation when compared to age-matched controls, in line with observed fat deposition defects in patients (Revêchon et al., 2017; Figure 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 4A–C and citation to Revêchon et al., 2017.

claim: Gene ontology terms related to blood vessels show upregulation of blood vessel morphogenesis in young HGPS patients.
source: Gene ontology terms related to blood vessels show upregulation of blood vessel morphogenesis, but a decrease of blood vessel maturation when comparing samples from young patients to either age-matched or old controls (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: Gene ontology terms related to blood vessels show a decrease of blood vessel maturation when comparing samples from young patients to either age-matched or old controls.
source: Gene ontology terms related to blood vessels show upregulation of blood vessel morphogenesis, but a decrease of blood vessel maturation when comparing samples from young patients to either age-matched or old controls (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: Blood vessel phenotype persists in comparisons between teen aged patients and their age-matched controls.
source: This phenotype persists in comparisons between teen aged patients and their age-matched controls (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Both young and teen-aged patient samples show a marked upregulation of genes in pathways related to muscle development and cardiac muscle differentiation and development when comparing both HGPS cohorts against adult controls.
source: Further, in a possible contribution to the circulatory defects observed in HGPS patients, both young and teen-aged patient samples show a marked upregulation of genes in pathways related to muscle development and cardiac muscle differentiation and development when comparing both HGPS cohorts against adult controls (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 6A–C.

source: Table 2. Number of up/down-regulated genes in young patient cohort comparisons.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in Table 2.

source: Table 2. Number of up/down-regulated genes in young patient cohort comparisons.

claim: About forty percent of genes upregulated in early infant patients when compared against their age matched controls are related to epigenetic modifications.
source: In this analysis, about forty percent of genes upregulated in early infant patients when compared against their age matched controls are related to epigenetic modifications as described in the previous analysis (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is based on the gene ontology analysis of the early infant cohort.

claim: The GO term 'HDACs deacetylate histones' shows the highest enrichment in the early infant patient group.
source: Specifically, the GO term 'HDACs deacetylate histones' shows the highest enrichment in this group.
evidence: The claim is based on the gene ontology analysis of the early infant cohort.

claim: The comparison of patients aged 4–7 years to their age matched controls show an enrichment for ossification and calcium homeostasis.
source: In contrast, the comparison of patients aged 4–7 years to their age matched controls show an enrichment for ossification and calcium homeostasis.
evidence: The claim is based on the gene ontology analysis of the 4-7 year old cohort.

claim: About 10% of genes downregulated in the 4-7 year old comparison are related to early chondrogenesis events.
source: Out of the cohort of genes identified as downregulated in this comparison (102), about 10% are related to early chondrogenesis events.
evidence: The claim is based on the gene ontology analysis of the 4-7 year old cohort.

claim: Parathyroid hormone related protein (PTHLH), insulin like growth factor (IGF1), bone morphogenic protein receptor 1B (BMPR1B), and collagen 10a1 (COL10a1) are an integral part of early commitment and control necessary for the triggering of endochondral ossification.
source: Among those, parathyroid hormone related protein (PTHLH), insulin like growth factor (IGF1), bone morphogenic protein receptor 1B (BMPR1B), and collagen 10a1 (COL10a1), are an integral part of early commitment and control necessary for the triggering of endochondral ossification (Bradley and Drissi, 2010; Green et al., 2015; Maruyama et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Bradley and Drissi, 2010; Green et al., 2015; Maruyama et al., 2010).

claim: Upregulated genes in age-matched and adult comparisons include BMP4, and several genes related to WNT5a biology which play an important role in skeletal development.
source: Further, upregulated genes in age-matched and adult comparisons include BMP4, and several genes related to WNT5a biology which play an important role in skeletal development (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene expression analysis shown in Figure 7A–C.

claim: Progeria fibroblasts show a decrease in telomere interactions.
source: At a whole chromosome folding level, we note that progeria fibroblasts show a decrease in telomere interactions and an apparent loss of 'Rabl' like structure (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Hi-C analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Progeria fibroblasts show an apparent loss of 'Rabl' like structure.
source: At a whole chromosome folding level, we note that progeria fibroblasts show a decrease in telomere interactions and an apparent loss of 'Rabl' like structure (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Hi-C analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Rabl structure loss was previously observed after DNA damage in fibroblasts.
source: This type of Rabl structure loss was previously observed after DNA damage in fibroblasts (Sanders et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sanders et al., 2020.

claim: Topologically associating domain (TAD) structure is preserved in Progeria fibroblasts.
source: We find that topologically associating domain (TAD) structure is preserved in Progeria fibroblasts, with even an increase in TAD boundary strength as compared to healthy parent controls (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Hi-C analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Progeria fibroblasts show an increase in TAD boundary strength as compared to healthy parent controls.
source: We find that topologically associating domain (TAD) structure is preserved in Progeria fibroblasts, with even an increase in TAD boundary strength as compared to healthy parent controls (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Hi-C analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: A similar increase in TAD boundary strength was previously found in senescent and progerin-expressing human mesenchymal progenitor cells.
source: A similar increase in TAD boundary strength was previously found in senescent and progerin-expressing human mesenchymal progenitor cells (Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2022.

claim: Increased TAD boundary strength was previously observed in DNA damaged fibroblasts.
source: Increased TAD boundary strength was also previously observed in DNA damaged fibroblasts (Sanders et al., 2020), suggesting that some of these features of genome structure may relate to the increased constitutive levels of DNA damage observed in these patient fibroblasts.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sanders et al., 2020.

claim: Some features of genome structure may relate to the increased constitutive levels of DNA damage observed in HGPS patient fibroblasts.
source: Increased TAD boundary strength was also previously observed in DNA damaged fibroblasts (Sanders et al., 2020), suggesting that some of these features of genome structure may relate to the increased constitutive levels of DNA damage observed in these patient fibroblasts.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similarity between HGPS genome structure and DNA damaged fibroblasts.

claim: The genome-wide compartment identity remains consistent among cohorts, with small changes in compartment identity appearing sporadically.
source: Interestingly, although the compartmentalization strength appears to be altered, the genome-wide compartment identity remains consistent among cohorts, with small changes in compartment identity appearing sporadically (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Hi-C compartment analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: There is a predominant loss of A compartment strength in the late passage HGPS cells.
source: Our results show that in the parent fibroblasts there are small changes in compartment strength (the degree of preference for interactions within the same compartment vs. between different compartments). In contrast, there is a predominant loss of A compartment strength in the late passage HGPS cells (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Hi-C compartment analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The loss of compartment strength at later passages in Progeria cells is consistent with previous observations.
source: The loss of compartment strength at later passages in Progeria cells is consistent with previous observations, though this more deeply sequenced, and less noisy dataset shows that compartments are more preserved in Progeria cells than previously observed (McCord et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McCord et al., 2013.

claim: Compartments are more preserved in Progeria cells than previously observed.
source: The loss of compartment strength at later passages in Progeria cells is consistent with previous observations, though this more deeply sequenced, and less noisy dataset shows that compartments are more preserved in Progeria cells than previously observed (McCord et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to previous data (McCord et al., 2013) and the current Hi-C data.

claim: Genes that are upregulated in HGPS tend to be located in the A compartment in both HGPS and WT fibroblast samples.
source: We found that genes that are upregulated in HGPS tend to be located in the A compartment in both HGPS and WT fibroblast samples, suggesting that many expression increases do not require chromosome compartment shifts (Figure 8F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by the compartment analysis of differentially expressed genes shown in Figure 8F–H.

claim: Many expression increases in HGPS do not require chromosome compartment shifts.
source: We found that genes that are upregulated in HGPS tend to be located in the A compartment in both HGPS and WT fibroblast samples, suggesting that many expression increases do not require chromosome compartment shifts (Figure 8F–H).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that upregulated genes remain in the A compartment.

claim: A subset of the genes that are downregulated in the 0–7 HGPS fibroblasts vs. normal age-matched or adult fibroblasts also shift toward the B compartment in HGPS samples compared to healthy adults.
source: In contrast, a subset of the genes that are downregulated in the 0–7 HGPS fibroblasts vs. normal age- matched or adult fibroblasts also shift toward the B compartment in HGPS samples compared to healthy adults. (Figure 8F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by the compartment analysis of differentially expressed genes shown in Figure 8F–H.

claim: Differences between all groups in Lamin association values are significant, with HGPS Lamin A association values markedly higher than their control counterparts.
source: We observe that differences between all groups are significant, with HGPS Lamin A association values markedly higher than their control counterparts (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B, Kruskal-Wallis p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by LAD analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B with statistical test (Kruskal-Wallis p<0.001).

claim: There is an overall dampening of the lamin association signal in HGPS patients.
source: However, we found that this shift in Lamin association is true throughout all genomic regions, with an overall dampening of the lamin association signal in HGPS patients (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C) and small regions switching from associated to dissociated from the nuclear lamina.
evidence: The claim is supported by LAD analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Normal fibroblast cells show a characteristic bimodal distribution in LAD intensity around markedly positive (LAD) and negative (non-LAD) values.
source: Comparing normal fibroblast cells HGADFN168 (belonging to the father of an HGPS patient) and HFFc6 (human foreskin fibroblast), we observe that both show a characteristic bimodal distribution in LAD intensity around markedly positive (LAD) and negative (non-LAD) values (log2 Lamin/input).
evidence: The claim is supported by LAD analysis comparing normal fibroblast cell lines.

claim: LAD values for the HGPS fibroblasts HGADFN167 show a normal distribution around zero.
source: In contrast, LAD values for the HGPS fibroblasts HGADFN167 show a normal distribution around zero: the intensity of both types of association is reduced in HGPS cells, consistent with an overall misregulated interaction between chromosomes and the nuclear lamina (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by LAD analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The intensity of both types of LAD association is reduced in HGPS cells, consistent with an overall misregulated interaction between chromosomes and the nuclear lamina.
